You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.
Usually, when you use the Simple Past tense, the time of the finished action is clear from the context or explicitly mentioned in the sentence.

For example:
Last week I went grocery shopping at my local grocery store.
Here, it is clear when the action of “going” happened (last week) and that it finished in that time period.

Here is another example:
Two weeks ago, I threw out a lot of garbage and I realized that I was producing too much waste.
Remember that there are both regular and irregular verbs. Look at the chart for examples of the Simple Past tense verbs.

The Passive: The Present Continuous and Present Perfect Tenses

You use the Present Continuous to talk about an action that is happening at the time of speaking. The action or event is in progress.
These large dumping sites are also causing contamination of groundwater, and making the water supplies unsafe.

You use the Present Perfect to talk about a finished action or event with present consequences. There is a connection between what happened in the past and the present.
People have become active participants in the recycling process.

You often choose the passive form when you want to talk about an action but are not so interested in saying who or what does/did it. Passives without agents (the doers) are common in academic and scientific writing.

images.text:
Last time I went food shopping, I thought about all the garbage that comes from just a simple bag of groceries - the majority of our shopping bag is easily disposable and ends up in the trash.
The question of what to do with all the refuse we produce has been asked repeatedly. Existing landfills are being filled up and have no capacity to hold more trash. These large dumping sites are also causing contamination of groundwater, and making the water supplies unsafe. Parts of the oceans have been polluted due to trash that is being dumped into the water by factories and individuals.

As concern for the environment grew, along with awareness of the dwindling supply of natural resources such as trees, recycling has provided us with the answer. Recycling has taken hold in major cities around the world. Recycling shares a simple principle: finding new uses for the things we no longer want.
Thanks to recycling, people have been made aware of the alternative ways to discard their trash, and have become active participants in the recycling process.

In many communities, the collection of the recyclable items is being organized by the local government. Newspapers, jars, plastic bottles, and aluminum cans are being separated and sorted into different bins. At the recycling center, the materials are sold to manufacturers to use again in the production of other items.
By giving your shopping bag a second thought, you are giving the environment a second chance.
